activity.instruction: Tap each glowing circle to learn how a zinc–copper cell makes electricity.
activity.intro: This cell turns a chemical reaction into electricity. Tap each part to see what it does.

hotspots.label: Zinc: the anode
hotspots.text: Zinc atoms lose electrons and go into the solution as Zn²⁺ ions. Losing electrons is oxidation, and it happens at the anode, the negative terminal here.

hotspots.label: Copper: the cathode
hotspots.text: Cu²⁺ ions from the solution gain electrons and coat the rod as copper metal. Gaining electrons is reduction, and it happens at the cathode.

hotspots.label: Salt bridge
hotspots.text: A tube of a salt such as KNO₃ in jelly. Its ions move to keep both solutions electrically neutral and complete the circuit.

hotspots.label: Voltmeter
hotspots.text: With 1 M solutions at 25 °C, it reads about 1.10 V. This is the standard cell potential, E°cell.

hotspots.label: Electron flow
hotspots.text: Electrons travel through the wire from zinc to copper. Inside the cell, ions carry the charge.

hotspots.label: Copper sulfate solution
hotspots.text: As Cu²⁺ ions turn into copper metal, the blue colour slowly fades. Overall: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.

activity.doneText: You know how a galvanic cell works!

solution.title: Worked solution
solution.note: At 25 °C. The reaction is Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, so two electrons move each time (n = 2).

predict.text: Both solutions are 1 M, so E = {E:2} V. If the copper solution is diluted to 0.1 M, the voltage will…
predict.explain: It fell to {E:3} V. Fewer Cu²⁺ ions means less push for the reaction, so the voltage drops.

predict.text: Back to 1 M each. Now the zinc solution is diluted to 0.01 M. The voltage will…
predict.explain: It rose to {E:3} V. Less product (Zn²⁺) means the forward reaction is favoured more.

goals.text: With Zn²⁺ at 0.5 M, make the cell read exactly 1.100 V.
goals.say: Equal concentrations give the standard voltage, 1.10 volts.

goals.text: Make the cell read 1.130 V (about 0.03 V above standard).
goals.say: Copper ten times more concentrated than zinc, for example 1 and 0.1 molar.

activity.doneText: You can use the Nernst equation!

activity.instruction: Order the metals from the strongest reducing agent to the weakest.
activity.intro: Some metals give away electrons much more easily than others. Order them from the most eager to the least.

items.say: Magnesium, minus 2.36 volts. It loses electrons most easily.
Silver, plus 0.80 volts. It holds on to its electrons best.

activity.hintWrong: Think: which metal gives away electrons more easily?
activity.doneText: That's the electrochemical series! The lower the standard reduction potential, the stronger the reducing agent.

activity.instruction: Move each electrolysis setup onto what it produces.
activity.intro: In electrolysis, electricity drives a reaction that would not happen by itself.
pairs: In molten salt, sodium ions gain electrons and become sodium metal.
In water, it is easier to reduce water than sodium ions, so hydrogen forms.
Chloride ions lose electrons and form chlorine gas.
The copper anode itself is oxidised. This is how copper is purified.

pairs.text: Dilute H₂SO₄ with a platinum anode

pairs: Water is oxidised at the anode, giving oxygen.

activity.instruction: Tap the best answer. Read why after each question.
activity.intro: Time for a quick quiz on this chapter.

questions.q: E° for Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V and for Zn²⁺/Zn is −0.76 V. What is E°cell for the zinc–copper cell?
In a galvanic cell, oxidation takes place at the…
questions.explain: Oxidation (losing electrons) always happens at the anode.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell, electrons flow through the wire from the cathode to the anode.
questions.explain: Electrons leave the anode, where they are released by oxidation, and flow to the cathode.

questions.q: What is the main job of the salt bridge?
options: Keep both solutions neutral and complete the circuit
questions.explain: Ions from the bridge move into each beaker to balance the charge, so the reaction can keep going.

questions.assertion: A zinc rod placed in copper sulfate solution becomes coated with copper.
questions.reason: Zinc has a lower standard reduction potential than copper.
questions.explain: Both are true. Zinc gives away electrons more easily, so it displaces copper from the solution.

questions.q: Brine (aqueous NaCl) is electrolysed. What forms at the cathode?
questions.explain: Water is reduced more easily than Na⁺ ions, so hydrogen gas forms at the cathode.

questions.q: About how much charge is one mole of electrons?
questions.explain: One faraday, about 96,500 coulombs, is the charge on one mole of electrons.

questions.q: Using Ag⁺/Ag (+0.80 V) and Zn²⁺/Zn (−0.76 V), what is E°cell?
questions.explain: Silver is the cathode: E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V.
